chapter_theme: Civakan grows up in Kantukkatan's house, is initiated into letters as a marriage to the maiden Knowledge and masters every art, so that all women long for him; his teacher then preaches the Jain path, the net of Death and the fence of vows, Civakan takes refuge in the Arhat and the three jewels, and the teacher leads him apart to reveal his royal birth.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by a merchant, who wins eight brides, regains his father's kingdom and renounces
the merchant who takes up and raises the newborn Civakan
the five nurses who bring up the child Civakan
the ascetic teacher who instructs Civakan in learning and doctrine and reveals his birth (unnamed in these verses)
the women of the city's streets and houses
the courtesans of Rajamapuram's pleasure quarter
Saccandan's minister, given the rule, who usurps it

363.reading: Guarded by five nurses bright as golden creepers, the lord rides cart, golden chariot and elephant, scattering wealth, and grows in excellence day by day.
363.nuance: ஐவர் are the five nurses of a royal child; the merchant's foster son is raised with a prince's train, though no one yet knows his birth.
363.event: The boy Civakan grows up under five nurses, riding out in carts, chariots and on elephants and scattering wealth.

364.reading: Like a lotus of the pools, like the moon that delights every eye, like a killing lion's cub, Civakan goes about praised by the world.
364.nuance: தெய்வப் பகை வென்றே at the close is unclear: it may say he has overcome the enmity of fate that struck his father, or only that he outshines the gods; the line does not settle it.

365.reading: Kantukkatan, giving gems, pearls, gold and coral like rain to all who ask, is like the wishing tree beyond count, and Sunandai is like a creeper of joy.
365.event: Kantukkatan pours out gifts to all who ask while Sunandai rejoices.

366.reading: Outshining fine gold, swimming ever further into a wealth of right conduct and praised by those rich in wisdom, the boy is like the beloved son of the brahmin of the first age.
366.nuance: Who ஆதி காலத்து அந்தணன் is the line does not say: it may be the first lord of the Jain tradition, whose son is the model of a prince, or Brahma; the comparison sets up the schooling that follows.

367.reading: The boy's good mother, bowing like a golden creeper, says that the child who breaks the bonds of women's hearts and troubles Kama himself should now go through the rite of the ink.
367.nuance: மை ஆடுக is read here as the anointing or ink rite that opens schooling, which the next two verses carry out; நற்றாய் would normally mean the birth mother, but in this house it can only be Sunandai, and the lament of பூமகள் is obscure.
367.event: Civakan's mother proposes the rite that begins his learning.

368.reading: The father of strong drum-like shoulders and fierce bow and the mother of bangled arms set about wedding their sweet-voiced child to the maiden called Knowledge.
368.nuance: Learning is figured as a bride (குமரி): the first of Civakan's unions is with knowledge, before the eight marriages that name the later ilampakams, and the chapter's own name, நாமகள், is the goddess of learning.
368.event: Kantukkatan and Sunandai resolve to have Civakan taught.

369.reading: Spreading gold, gems, pearls and coin by the measure, and setting out every offering, they wrote on a gold leaf with a gold stylus from a gold seat and joined the lady Learning to the boy.
369.event: Civakan is initiated into letters with a writing on a golden leaf amid heaped offerings.

370.reading: Drinking in all the beauty of the goddess of learning, mastering every weapon art beginning with the arrow and reaching the far shore of the field Kama made, he shone on earth like its forehead mark.
370.event: Civakan masters the books, all the arts of arms and the arts of love.

371.reading: Women with waists slender as lightning, their skin flooded with the pallor of longing, melt for the saffron-shouldered youth like cows whose calves have been hidden.
371.event: The women of the city pale and melt with longing for Civakan.

372.reading: Even the courtesans who sell their bodies at a price, with eyes fiercer than spears, who live by marking young men's chests with their breasts, cry for Civakan night and day and cannot bear it.
372.nuance: The verse sets the women who trade love among those undone by him: the youth's beauty overturns even a desire that is for sale.
372.event: The courtesans of the city lament day and night with longing for Civakan.

373.reading: When the teacher had given without stint everything he himself had tasted, as if a flood of heavenly nectar had gathered there, he set out to speak one word of counsel to Prince Civakan.
373.nuance: The teacher is not named in this chapter; the verse only says he gave all he had gathered. உறுதி, counsel for the boy's lasting good, opens a sermon that runs to 379.
373.event: The teacher, having taught Civakan all he knows, begins to give him counsel.

374.reading: The teacher says that one who examines by the way of the books, enters into them subtly, puts away the many paths of evil and joins the virtue that holds to the path of the Lord who is like the sun, is nectar to good souls in the four states.
374.nuance: நால் நெறி வகையில் நின்ற நல் உயிர் is read as the souls of the four states of birth (gods, humans, animals, hell-beings), which would make the claim Jain; பருதி அம் கடவுள் அன்ன கோன் is the Lord like the sun, not the sun himself.

claims.claim: one who follows scripture, gives up evil and holds to the Lord's path is nectar to souls in all four states of being

375.reading: Those great in knowledge reach the path where hard deeds wear away and stand in a full sea of bliss, while those burnt by the frenzied fields of the five-mouthed fire-snake called the senses stand in a sea of pain.
375.nuance: The senses (பொறி) are one snake with five mouths breathing fire, not five separate beasts; the two seas, bliss and pain, are the two ends of the one choice.

claims.claim: by knowledge one reaches the path on which hard karma is worn away, and stands in bliss
those given over to the five senses stand in a sea of suffering

376.reading: Death, cruel, has laid with his killing tools a net no one can undo; we who know he has laid it do not know how to escape it by austerity and go our way, but gaze on the world's pleasures: are we pitiable, or are we great?
376.nuance: The closing question is ironic: பெரியமே, 'we are great', mocks those who know the net and stay in it; the speaker counts himself among them (நாமும்).

claims.claim: only austerity frees one from the net Death has laid, yet those who know it still turn to pleasure

377.reading: We have rarely won the nectar that splits all great sorrow and ends birth, yet do not know how to take its fruit; pampering the five senses while our days pass, can we achieve what we intended when the fierce fire takes us?
377.nuance: கூர் எரி கவரும் போழ்து is the cremation fire: the limit is set by the burning of the body, not by the onset of dying.

claims.claim: the teaching that ends birth is rarely won and must be used before death, since nothing can be done once the pyre takes the body

378.reading: Even if one proclaims the truth with the sounding drum and explains it clearly before the revellers, can one make those of drunken mind, bent on sinking into roaring hell-fire, take the vows of virtue?
378.nuance: குணவதம் is a named class of the Jain layman's vows; the teacher's despair of the many sets off the one pupil who will take them in 380.

claims.claim: those bent on hell cannot be brought to take the vows even when the truth is proclaimed to them

379.reading: Ploughmen, if you would not lose the crop sown as pearls in the coral-mouthed field, sprouting as an infant, bearing its ear in youth and ripening in old age, set the fence of conduct against the many disease-bringing beasts that graze, he said.
379.nuance: The vocative உழவிர்காள் makes every hearer a farmer of his own life; சீல after குணவதம் in 378 names the second class of the Jain layman's vows, so the fence is not general virtue but vowed discipline.

claims.claim: a life from infancy to old age must be fenced with the discipline of the vows against the beasts that bring sickness

380.reading: Because the deed of old, which lifts one from the falling states and leads to the bright golden world, drove him, and because his understanding went forth and shone, the youth with gem ornaments like the rayed moon took refuge in the Wise One, a raft on the deep sea.
380.nuance: Two causes are given side by side, ஊழ் வினை துரத்தலானும் உணர்வு சென்று எறித்தலானும: the past deed drives, and his own understanding also reaches out; karma here is a good one that pushes toward release, the reverse of the destiny that drove his father to ruin.
380.event: Civakan takes refuge in the Arhat.

claims.claim: a ripening good deed of the past together with the dawning of one's own understanding brings one to refuge in the Arhat

381.reading: Fitting the jewelled door of knowledge in the frame of right seeing and sliding in the diamond bolt called conduct, he shut all the evil states and opened the way to climb to the world of boundless bliss.
381.nuance: காட்சி, ஞானம், ஒழுக்கம் are the Jain three jewels, built into one door: faith is the frame, knowledge the door, conduct the bolt; the same door that shuts the lower births opens the upper world.
381.event: Civakan takes up right faith, knowledge and conduct.

claims.claim: right seeing, knowledge and conduct together close the evil states of birth and open the way to boundless bliss

382.reading: To the youth who had become lord of good dharma, reached the fourfold refuge and taken on the ancient bond of dharma, the teacher explained without darkness how men on base paths of dharma have erred about the truth, and all the nature of the householder's dharma.
382.nuance: நால்வகைச் சரணம் is the fourfold refuge of the Jain creed. The participles of lines 1 and 2 could describe the teacher rather than Civakan; read with 380, they fit the new convert. The teaching given to him is the householder's dharma, not the monk's.
382.event: The teacher instructs Civakan in the errors of false paths and in the householder's dharma.

383.reading: Taking Civakan away from the band of youths with their fiery spears, the teacher went to a grove of chosen flowers, as if roofed with woven garlands, to make plain to him his birth.
383.nuance: பிறப்பினைத் தெருட்டல் is both the secret of his royal birth and, after 375 to 381, a lesson on birth itself.
383.event: The teacher leads Civakan apart into a flower grove to tell him of his birth.

384.reading: Making sure no myna, parrot or any creature kings use as spies was near, and seated in splendour on a flower seat in the shade of the ashoka's tender leaves, he said to the archer: hear this matter.
384.nuance: The care against talking birds shows that the secret is still dangerous: the usurper rules and the heir's birth is unknown.
384.event: The teacher checks the grove for spies and, seated under an ashoka, bids Civakan listen.

385.reading: The teacher begins: Saccandan was king of the world, and his queen was Vijayai; the king, having thought it through, sent the queen away on the machine, and was swallowed by the unlearned minister of deluded heart.
385.nuance: The teacher's retelling compresses the whole of the king's fall into one verse and lays it on the minister's lack of learning (கல்லா மந்திரி) and delusion, not on the king's pleasure or on fate.
385.event: The teacher tells Civakan how his father Saccandan sent Queen Vijayai away on the flying machine and was killed by his minister.

links.note: In 200 the narrator introduces Kattiyankaran as a man of flawless learning (வெளிறு இலாக் கேள்வியான்); in 385 the teacher, telling the story to the son, calls him the unlearned minister (கல்லா மந்திரி).
links.teaches: The same minister's learning is affirmed by the narrator at his rise and denied by the teacher after his crime, so the epic counts learning by its fruit in conduct, not by what a man has heard.

links.note: In 215 a destiny formed before (முனம் ஆகிய பான்மை) sprouts in Saccandan and drives him after the queen to his ruin; in 380 the old deed (ஊழ் வினை) drives his son to refuge in the Arhat.
links.teaches: The epic uses one mechanism, a ripened past deed pushing a man, to drown the father in pleasure and lift the son to the Jina, and only the son's case adds his own understanding as a second cause.

links.note: Vijayai dreamt in 223 that the ashoka (பிண்டி) fell and a shoot rose from its foot; in 384 the teacher sits in the shade of an ashoka to tell that shoot of the felled tree.
links.teaches: The heir learns of his father's fall under the very tree that figured the fall in his mother's dream, so the revelation scene closes the dream's image on its fulfilment.

links.note: Naladiyar 331 shows people revelling in the world's net while Death waits to seize them, like a turtle sporting in the pot over the fire; Cintamani 376 makes Death the one who laid the net and the revellers people who know it is there.
links.teaches: Set beside the quatrain, the epic's step is to take away the excuse of ignorance: the turtle does not know its state, but the teacher's 'we' know Death's net and still turn to pleasure, so folly becomes a failure of will.

gains.a: the teacher's irony (பெரியமே) is sharpened by the quatrain's ignorant turtle, against which knowing captives look worse
gains.b: the quatrain's net and killer gain an agent who sets the snare deliberately and an exit it does not name, austerity

links.note: Kural 348 says that those who have wholly renounced have reached the head and all others are caught in the net; Cintamani 376 names the net as Death's and austerity (நோற்று) as the way out of it.
links.teaches: The couplet divides men into renouncers and the netted, while the epic shows the netted as knowing their state, so renunciation is not only clear seeing but a doing that knowledge alone does not bring.

gains.a: the epic's net is tied to the Kural's chapter on renunciation, making நோற்று the renouncer's act
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'net' is given an owner, Death, and a cause for staying in it, the pull of pleasure

links.note: Kural 335 bids good deeds be rushed before the hiccup stops the tongue; Cintamani 377 asks whether anything intended can be done when the fire takes the body, after the teaching that ends birth has been rarely won.
links.teaches: The couplet's urgency rests on how near death may be; the epic adds that the means of release is already in hand and wasted by pampering the senses, so delay is the squandering of a rare gain and not only a race with death.

gains.a: the teacher's rhetorical question is grounded in a rule, act before the end
gains.b: the couplet's general 'good deed' is specified as using a teaching already obtained, and its limit moved from the death rattle to the pyre

links.note: Kural 6 says that those who stand on the path of the one who quenched the five senses live long; Cintamani 375 sets those who reach the path that wears away hard deeds in a sea of bliss and those burnt by the five-mouthed snake of the senses in a sea of pain.
links.teaches: Where the couplet promises long life on the path of one who quenched the senses, the Jain teacher makes the reward the wearing away of karma and the penalty a sea of suffering, turning a blessing of the householder into a choice between release and pain.

gains.a: the epic's senses-snake and its path are tied to the Kural's opening praise of the one who quenched the five
gains.b: the couplet's 'long life' is shown read by a Jain teacher as the destruction of karma, a reading its words allow but do not state

links.note: Both build a field guarded by a fence against stray beasts: Cintamani 379's crop is life from infancy to old age, its beasts diseases and its fence the vows (சீல வேலி); Pattinattar's field is the heart, its cattle the five senses, its fence calm (சாந்த வேலி), and its fruit Siva's form.
links.teaches: The shared Tamil figure of the fenced crop carries opposite ends: the Jain teacher fences a life to be kept from harm by vowed discipline, while the Saiva poet fences a devotion that ripens into the god, so the doctrine lies in what each names as fence and fruit.

gains.a: the teacher's brief farm image is seen as a choice: he fences life itself and names no fruit beyond it
gains.b: Pattinattar's devotional field is set against a Jain version where no grace ripens, showing his fruit of the five letters as the Saiva addition

links.note: Tirumanthiram 1527: when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru, and when one's own agency ends the impurities go; Cintamani 380: a past good deed drives Civakan and his own understanding reaches out, and he takes refuge in the Arhat.
links.teaches: Both put a teacher at the turn toward release, but for Tirumular the teacher is grace descending once deeds cancel and one's agency ends, while for the Jain epic it is the push of a good deed and the youth's own understanding that bring him to the teacher's Lord.

gains.a: Civakan's conversion is shown to need no descent of grace: karma and his own understanding suffice
gains.b: the Saiva claim that one's own agency must end is set against a release story in which agency is one of its two causes

links.note: Kural 49 calls the householder's life itself what is named virtue; in Cintamani 382 the teacher, once Civakan has taken the Jain refuge, teaches him the householder's dharma alongside the errors of false paths.
links.teaches: The Jain teacher does not set renunciation against the household here but gives the new convert the householder's dharma as his first instruction, so the epic holds the Kural's household virtue as a stage inside the path to release rather than its rival.

gains.a: the content of the teacher's instruction, left unstated, is placed against the Kural's account of what household virtue is
gains.b: the couplet's praise of household life is seen kept, but subordinated, by a tradition whose hero will renounce at the end

source_issues: Verses 368 to 385 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 367 line 3 (பூமகள் புலம்பி வைக) and line 2 (மை ஆடுக) are obscure as printed; verse 364 line 4 (தெய்வப் பகை வென்றே) is unclear.
